utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Simic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are continuing with cross-examination by the Prosecution of Mr. Savo Popovic. Yes. We have to wait for the witness. I'm sure he's still coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm informed we have to wait a few minutes for the connection to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please use this opportunity to -- I have just received the last two statements from the Translation Unit, the bis 92 statements, so we would please like the opportunity now for witnesses Djordje Tubakovic and Stojan Damjanovic to hand in their statements. So if Mr. Usher could please hand out the documents to the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. The first statement is a bis 92 statement by witness Djordje Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, for identification only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will get the numbers later. You can go ahead with the next statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The last 92 bis witness whose statement we would like to give the Chamber is a statement by Stojan Damjanovic. We have now disclosed all 92 bis statements as concern the defence of Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would it be better to deal with the Simeunovic witness now, the live witness, and get that completed? It's just some re-cross-examination and re-direct, and then finish with this sometime later this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe if I may address. This is unfortunately not possible, because having in mind that we have this witness on videolink, we advise the Victims and Witness Section to bring Mr. Simeunovic only after 10.00. So he's not here at the moment. It's a good suggestion, but we did not really have the idea that this is going to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we'll wait. We'll wait another few minutes and see if we can get connected.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Good morning. We are trying to resolve a problem. It shouldn't take more than a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask the Prosecution: On these two statements under Rule 92 bis, how long they think they need for the two statements? I thought they would be able to indicate whether or not -- whatever their position is by Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall go ahead and get the numbers for the statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first statement and the witness's first and last name is Djordje Tubakovic. That would be marked D184/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. ID for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the next statement, the witness's first and last name, Stojan Damjanovic would be marked as D185/3 and ter ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] I think that for the moment we can start with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Popovic. We shall continue with cross-examination by the Prosecution. Please, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Popovic. You testified last Thursday --

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified last Thursday that 16 non-Serb civilians were murdered at Crkvina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't get it. 60? Did you say 60.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't testify as to the number. I said that I was not present, and I didn't count, as has been suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you testified that a number of non-Serb men or civilians were murdered at Crkvina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that we had information that a heinous crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. You had information and you used the term horrendous, that there was a horrendous event and that a number of non-Serb men were killed; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in a small municipality such as Samac, the murder of a number of men is a major event. You referred to it as a horrendous event.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you learned of this a few days after it occurred. That's what you testified to.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff, you said, also learned about this a few days after it occurred.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And due to its significance and awfulness, or if you want to say disgusting nature of killing a number of people, it wasn't hard to learn about this event; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was kept secret, and that's why the true information never reached the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that due to the horrendous nature of the event, people knew all about this, or people knew that it had occurred, a number of non-Serb civilians were killed in Crkvina? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't think I've understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that due to the horrendous nature and the fact that a large number of people were killed or murdered, it was common knowledge that this incident had occurred in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I emphasised a moment ago that the information concerning this horrendous crime was eventually found out several days later. That's when I found out about it, and I said that several days later we were told that there was an investigation into the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And several days later, you said a few days later previously, people knew about it because it was a notorious event. People knew about it, including the Crisis Staff, a few or several days later; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that already. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the Crisis Staff learned, a few days later, about this event. Was this -- and that this was a subject of discussion at the Crisis Staff. At how many Crisis Staff meetings in May was this matter discussed? Two, three, four, five? How many meetings?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer this now how many meetings exactly. After those events, I found out that there had been an investigation, both by the civilian and by the military authorities. As far as I know, the public security station was in charge of that, and the military authorities too. I had no further information as to what they had done and how they had gone about the investigation, what the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, sir. My question is: How many Crisis Staff meetings? Was it more than one that this matter was discussed? More than one, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very accurate on this, whether it was at one or two or more of the meetings. It has been a long time, too long a time, perhaps, for me to specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, at this meeting or the meetings when this matter was discussed, do you recall if Blagoje Simic said anything about this incident?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he insisted energetically for the crime to be investigated and for the perpetrators to be brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about Simeon Simic, who was the press or information officer for the Crisis Staff? Did he have any comments, since this was a very -- since this was a major or a significant matter for Bosanski Samac? Did Simeon Simic say anything about it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, as to which of the members of the Crisis Staff said what, it's very difficult for me to recall precisely. I did not keep any personal record of the meetings which could assist me now to say exactly who said what. But I know that there was a condemnation of that crime and that we were shocked by what had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say we were shocked, that includes all the members of the Crisis Staff: Simeon Simic, Bozo Ninkovic, who was assisting Simeon Simic and was also assisting on technical matters, Miroslav Tadic, all the members were shocked and condemned it; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, even though you indicate that you condemn this incident, were any letters written to the military, the republican MUP, the SUP, the Republika Srpska government, concerning this incident or the protection of prisoners? Were any letters written after this incident?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't take any notes at those meetings. That was for the technical secretary or the lawyer who was involved. Whether they wrote letters to anyone or not, I can't say now. I can't remember. But I know that any conclusions from those meetings that were held were documented, and if that was forwarded to anyone in that case, they should have it, the army, the government, or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic has testified on the 21st of November, 2002, that no letters were ever sent in April, May, June, or July about the safety of the prisoners, no orders were issued, no letters were ever written. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Blagoje Simic was the president, and he was best placed to know. Whether he signed anything or not, whether anything was forwarded to anyone or not. If he said that nothing was, then that means nothing was ever sent. I was just a member who was present. I didn't dictate the documents that were drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So let's get this -- I just want to make sure this is correct. You've testified and Blagoje Simic has testified that numerous letters were sent to help the Serb prisoners in Odzak, but no letters were ever sent by the Crisis Staff to help the non-Serb prisoners in Samac; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at first, in Odzak, in the Odzak area, there were about 4.000 Serb detainees, mostly women and children, and that's why an appeal was sent out to all the factors to assist in liberating those people so that there would be no consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question was that letters were sent out on behalf of the Serb prisoners being held in Odzak, but no letters were sent on behalf of the non-Serb prisoners being held in Samac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Samac, a number of persons were detained and questioned as to whether they had taken part in armament, whether they had been members of any of the units, and I don't know why anyone should request an intervention by any of the international organisations, because that was simply the jurisdiction of the public security station and that's what the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is -- you can answer it yes or no: Letters were sent out on behalf of the Serbs of Odzak by the Crisis Staff, but the Crisis Staff sent out no letters to any public or international agency on behalf of the non-Serbs of Samac that were being detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did send a number of things in connection with the International Red Cross. But I think also those over there, when there was an international exchange, contacts were -- contact was made with the International Red Cross. Now, how exactly this was done, whether letters or appeals were sent out, I don't know, because that wasn't part of my job. So I can't specify as to what and how exactly was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're not aware of any letters that were sent out on behalf of the non-Serbs -- the non-Serbs of Samac that were being detained, letters concerning problems relating to their safety? No letters were ever sent out, according to Blagoje Simic. Is that also your view: No letters were sent out by --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's rather a suggestion to my learned friend not the objection. For the sake of the clarity of the transcript, maybe he can make reference of the page number of what exactly Blagoje Simic said and when, so that we can follow the accuracy. Because you mentioned that he testified on the 21st of November last year and on numerous occasions. I believe for the -- in order to clarify that, we have to have a number of transcript, page number, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure the Prosecution can --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 12583.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is again: Isn't it true that no letter was sent out by the Crisis Staff of Samac on behalf of the detained prisoners in Samac relating to their safety or their health, no letters were ever sent? That's what Blagoje Simic testified to. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak on Blagoje Simic's behalf, whether what he said was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, your memory: Do you recall any letters being sent out in April, May, or June, relating to the protection, health, and safety of the prisoners of the non-Serb prisoners being held in Samac? Do you recall any letters ever being sent? And when I say "being sent," by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I can't specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, sir. You testified last Thursday about an unprompted or spontaneous meeting which occurred at the PIK factory, the PIK company, and there was talk at that meeting about the need for a lawyer for the Crisis Staff. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Mirko Jovanovic was the president of the Executive Board, proposed a lawyer, Mitar Mitrovic, as they were both from Obudovac, they knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Mirko Jovanovic, who was an SDS member, proposed Mitar Mitrovic, who was also an SDS member; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether he was an SDS member or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified last week, at page 16306, that both Mirko Jovanovic and Mitar Mitrovic were SDS members. Do you wish to maintain that testimony or do you want to recant that at this point?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that he was an SDS member, but as far as my memory serves me, he may have been a radical. From these two options, I don't know whether he was SDS or radical. I don't know. Perhaps at the time when he was proposed which party he belonged to at that very moment when he was proposed, whether he was in the SDS or whether he was in the Radical Party, I don't know. But it would be one of these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, last week you testified: Mr. Mirko Jovanovic, who was a member of the SDS, and Mitar, as technical secretary, was a member of the SDS. That was your testimony. Do you still maintain that both of those individuals were members of the SDS or do you wish to change your testimony? Maybe something happened over the weekend that would make you change your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I do not wish to change my testimony. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified that you attended the Serbian Municipal Assembly meeting of March 28th, 1992. Do you recall that? Remember in Obudovac, where they had the elections? Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present as an observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, isn't it true at that meeting on March 28th, 1992, Mitar Mitrovic was appointed the secretary of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Samac, on that date? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take part. I was not a deputy of that assembly. I was an observer. I attended. I was present in the hall, among the others who came to see what was happening. So I can't say or claim 100 per cent what whoever from the elected got which appointment, whether they were elected as the secretary of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit P124 ter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you see that document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 19 in the English and page 9 in the B/C/S. Can you see it now, sir, section 10?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me read to you from the Official Gazette of the municipality of Samac, the same one that we were looking at last week: "Mitar Mitrovic B.L., is hereby appointed secretary of the Samac Municipal Assembly." That's Article 1. Article 2: "This notice shall be published in the official organ of the municipality." Date: March 28th, 1992, signed by Dusan Tanasic, vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. Based on what I just read to you, Mitar Mitrovic was appointed the secretary of the Samac Municipal Assembly three weeks prior to that April meeting that you talked about; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this decision, that can be seen, but I don't know when that decision was compiled, and probably because of that, Mirko Jovanovic as the president of the Executive Board, proposed Mr. -- this gentleman to come and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But all I'm saying, sir, is Mitar Mitrovic was appointed as secretary of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Samac three weeks prior to that meeting at the PIK; isn't that correct, based on what I read to you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, were you aware, on the day prior to that meeting, the day prior to that meeting which you attended on March 28th, the Municipal Assembly, that in Sarajevo, Radovan Karadzic ordered that crisis staffs be immediately established, and this was at the Serb Assembly: " The moment you arrive in your municipalities, you must urgently establish crisis staffs." Were you aware of that statement by Radovan Karadzic on the 27th of March, 1992, one day prior to the decision to establish the Crisis Staff at the local Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know about that. I wasn't aware of such a decision or an order that Karadzic furthered or forwarded --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the basis that to some extent this witness can be misled by this question. Page 13, line 3, 4, and 5. Maybe it can be rephrased, because otherwise it's unclear what my learned friend said one day prior to the decision to establish the Crisis Staff. Which decision? How he came to this conclusion? Maybe we can clarify that in the question. The question was not so clear, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel is taking the question out of context. He doesn't look at the part on page 12 that's right in front of it. But I'd be happy to clarify it a little bit too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's just taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Karadzic's speech was at the 14th assembly session of the assembly of Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina on March 27th, 1992, in Sarajevo, and on that date, Radovan Karadzic said: "You must -- the moment you arrive in your municipalities, you must urgently establish crisis staffs." He said that in a speech to the delegates. And on the following day, you know, as we discussed last week, that a decision was made in Obudovac to establish a municipal Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think it's another sort of manipulation of my learned friend. Where we have a document that in Obudovac the decision was made to create a Serbian Crisis Staff, and speaking of specifically date 28th of March because we are around that date. So maybe, in fairness to this witness, if my learned friend has some of this assumptions, he should show him where it says when it was adopted and then he can elicit the answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did that last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic, this witness attended the meetings. Most of these questions are within his knowledge, so let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you. But please, he's speaking on page 13, line 25, that the decision was made in Obudovac to establish a municipal Crisis Staff. And furthermore, he's relating to the date of 27th of March. We all know that certain discussion was made at the level of the Executive Board of the Serbian municipality, and it was two weeks later than this day. It was prior to the outbreak of the hostilities in the municipality. So my basis for my submission here and objection is that my learned friend is trying to confuse the witness, because there are two separate decisions of two separate organs, on two separate dates. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me read you Mr. Karadzic's statement: "We know that our people have armed themselves. We don't know the various ways and means by which this was done, but we do know that the people have enough weapons. I must say, however, that we do not have paramilitary units. When you return to your municipalities, especially the newly formed municipalities, I ask you to do what you are required and entitled to do under the law. The moment you arrive in your municipalities, you must urgently establish crisis staffs." Now, sir, you testified last week, or you agreed last week, based on looking at the Official Gazette that, on March 28th a decision was made to establish a Crisis Staff in Obudovac; isn't that correct, one day after Radovan Karadzic's speech to the Assembly of Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've presented a decision of the Executive Board, and I've told you about it. I was not present. I was not a member of the SDS or a deputy. You have to put in the context of the Municipal Assembly, and then I had the decision of the Executive Board presented to me. So what I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is: You testified last week -- you read those articles at that meeting that you attended in Obudovac, where the decision was made to establish a Crisis Staff, and that was -- that decision was on the 28th of March, 1992. Isn't that one day after Karadzic's speech on March 27th? Yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the first time -- that was the first time I saw such a decision, and I cannot state here yes or no. And I said the last time the same. I don't know why you're insisting now on it when I was not a participant. I was not a deputy at this assembly to say whether I was or not Executive Board member. I was not participating in the making of decisions. I said the first time here, when it was presented to me, that's when I saw such decisions. It's the first time here that I saw such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you if you were a member at that time. You admitted that you had attended that meeting. So isn't it fair to say that, based on what you read and what you observed, a plan was established for the -- a plan was ruled on to establish a Crisis Staff on the 28th of March, which was one day after Karadzic's speech? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about such a thing, and I cannot confirm that it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir. You testified last week about your brother-in-law, Colonel Mico Djordjevic [sic]; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's a relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you testified that he was commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade sometime in May of 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us: How old was he 11 years ago, when he commanded the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript, because it might be important. In page 16, line 16, instead of Djordjevic, it should be Djurdjevic, D-J-U, et cetera. Because we have two almost similar names here, Djordjevic Crni and Djurdjevic. So it might be of importance to clarify this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We should have the correct names, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how old he was 11 years ago, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have been in his 50s. Whether he was a couple of years older or younger than that, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, he wasn't aged or elderly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he is about my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At that time, he wasn't aged or elderly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends how you look at it, really. A person who is in his 50s or 60s or 40s, whether that person is old or not old, or that person has vitality or not. But let's say that he was not elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And he wasn't feeble-minded or mentally incompetent, sir; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, he was having no problems commanding the 2nd Posavina Brigade due to his age; isn't that correct? He wasn't too old to command?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in fact, he was given another post as commander of the 1st Brigade in Brcko, which was much larger; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the establishment, it was probably like that. That's what he told me. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said, "It was..." And I didn't get the last of your statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that for him it was to take over the command, over the 1st Posavina Brigade, was a lot more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in your Crisis Staff meetings you attended in May and June and let's say early June of 1992, did Crisis Staff members discuss any problems with Colonel Djurdjevic commanding his brigade, due to his age? Was that ever discussed in the Crisis Staff among the Crisis Staff members?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, if I was present, it was never in relation to his age, but there were certain problems that he brought up during a visit, that there was a pressure from the side of Crni, and his henchmen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, relating to age, strictly relating to age, were there any issues before the Crisis Staff indicating that he was too old to command? Did the Crisis Staff members among themselves discuss that at a meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't say that. Perhaps somebody said that, but not while I was present, because, of course, we were related in some way, so when I was present, nobody ever said a thing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did the Crisis Staff members, including yourself, Blagoje Simic, ever contact Colonel Dencic and indicate that they were having problems with Colonel Djurdjevic, Colonel Djurdjevic's command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, based on his age? Were any of those contacts made?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, as far as I know -- we were not in contact with Mr. Dencic. I never saw him. Personally, I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, well, you didn't, but did Blagoje Simic or any members of the Crisis Staff go and meet with Colonel Dencic, relating to problems of Colonel Djurdjevic's command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, due to his advanced age? Were there any of those types of meetings with Blagoje Simic or Simeon Simic with Colonel Dencic, or any members of the Crisis Staff that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said last time in relation to this that here you have to not take into consideration the Crisis Staff, because if Mr. Dencic gave him an order to go to the 1st Posavina Brigade, that he was too old for the 2nd and not for this one, then I said that in this part of the participation of changing the place of Mr. Djurdjevic, that was only Stevan Todorovic who had taken part in that, and Crni and all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Did the members of the Crisis Staff, including Blagoje Simic, a defendant in this case, or Miroslav Tadic, have meetings with Colonel Dencic relating to problems of Colonel Djurdjevic due to his advanced age was unable to command the 2nd Posavina Brigade? Are you aware of any meetings of that type?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the answer is no, they didn't meet for that. It is possible, though, that they did meet without telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir -- we've had testimony in this case from the defendant Blagoje Simic that he did in fact communicate with Colonel Dencic and have a meeting with him. I'd like to read to you just a section from the transcript of November 14th, 2002, at page 12300.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you communicate with Colonel Dencic? Blagoje Simic's answer: "Yes, once."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when was that and on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it had to do with the visit in Ugljevik and the pressure by the army too, that Colonel Djurdjevic, because of his advanced age, was no longer able to command the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the period beginning of June. Sir, did you attend that meeting with Blagoje Simic and Colonel Dencic where problems relating to Colonel Djurdjevic were discussed because of his advanced age, he was unable to command the 2nd Posavina Brigade? Did you attend that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you weren't even aware of that meeting being held in Ugljevik?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware. The first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, isn't it a fact that there were other things that they never told you that happened, just like that meeting? Not being an SDS member, you weren't informed prior to April 17th about the different policies and plans of the SDS; isn't that true, prior to April 17th?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the SDS; therefore, none of them informed me as a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So Blagoje Simic didn't discuss what orders he was receiving from the SDS leadership, he didn't discuss that with you prior to April 17th?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic didn't discuss with you what conversations he was having with the SDS leadership prior to April 17th?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you didn't know what, if any, conversations or meetings Blagoje Simic was having with the SDS leadership prior to April 17th, did you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're referring to. Do you mean the municipal leadership or a different level of leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The republican-level leadership: Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, the SDS Main Board.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you that I didn't take part in SDS party meetings, the events surrounding the setting up, the establishment of the municipality, I did follow, because I was interested, and I did attend those meetings, but not the rest of their meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you present in 1992 and 1993, when Blagoje Simic met or spoke with Karadzic or General Mladic? Were you present for any meetings or conversations?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Maybe this line of questions could be rephrased in order not to establish certain unfair positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, there is nothing wrong with this question. Will you stop interrupting the proceedings. There is nothing wrong with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He is being asked whether he was present. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but allegedly present, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Allegedly, that would be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness knows whether or not he was present and he will be able to answer. Will you please keep quiet and just sit down. Stop interrupting the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you present for any meetings or conversations between Blagoje Simic and Radovan Karadzic or General Mladic in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't know whether they had meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Blagoje Simic ever inform you or other members of the Crisis Staff about communications he had with the SDS Main Board or Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At meetings of the Executive Board, no such information was made public. That's as far as I can remember. This was ten years ago. I don't think any such information was disclosed. If there had been indeed any such information, this would have been kept within the limits of the close circle of the SDS members, and I was myself not a member. Therefore, I cannot be any more accurate than I've tried to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Intervention to the transcript. Page 22, line 12. Maybe something which -- I don't know what the witness exactly said, because the question was related to the Crisis Staff, and in his answer on page 22, line 12, he's speaking about Executive Board. So maybe we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your answer, you stated that at meetings of the Executive Board, no such information was made public. Did you mean the Crisis Staff, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff and the Executive Board were not the same thing. Therefore, whether the Executive Board discussed this or had information on it, because I was not a member of the Executive Board and I was not familiar with their procedures and with the items discussed at their meetings; therefore, that's why I'm saying that I cannot provide an answer here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when Biljana Plavsic stated that the leaders of the SDS and the Serb leaders provided direction to the municipal leaders, you can't tell us what information they provided to the SDS leadership, because you weren't part of the SDS in 1992 or 1993; isn't that correct? And I mean the SDS municipal leadership of Samac.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Since we're limited on time this morning, sir, let's move a little bit ahead to Odzak. You testified that while you were a member of the Crisis Staff, you were assigned to Odzak and you became a member of the civilian military council; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Executive Council, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, objection. I didn't hear that this witness testified that he was a member of civilian military council. He was a member of council of military administration, which is rather different. So maybe my learned friend can be precise with the constructions. And because he just provided me this morning one document, and he can find it on -- it's internal page 03003199, where the -- there is a translation that he was -- Mr. Popovic was president of council of military administration, or military administration council, anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's been referred to several different names, but let's just refer to it as the council, just to move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you were a member of this council, this military council; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, a member of the civilian council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you ask the witness -- he knows what the correct name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, what is the correct name of this council? We've had several names, the civilian military council, the civilian war council, the military council. What was the correct name, according to yourself?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names that we used, military council, executive council, civilian council. Because no document ever ascertained with accuracy, no military administration document, as to what the name of the council should actually be. There is no written document on that. The members of the council simply gave it a name. We christened it, in a manner of speaking, and we used those different names, in communication with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, you were involved in economic affairs on that council, sir, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, economic affairs, as far as the civilian sector is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And also in that council was Simo Zaric, a defendant in this case?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Zaric was added, that is, Simo Zaric and myself were told to go to Odzak and that there we would join the work on organising civilian life. This is the part of work that was assigned to me. And Simo had civilian and military intelligence work. We were supposed to have those areas of activity. And as far as I know, Simo established contact with security organs of the Tactical Group, that is, in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Simo did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you, sir, were more than just a council member. You were the president or the head of that council; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but no one ever said or wrote that. They simply came up to me and told me: You will head the council. Council will be appointed to include delegates across the local communes, and that's how I was promoted and became the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, other people, including Simo Zaric, have indicated that you were the president or head of that council, so people were aware that you were the head or president of that council; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You held that position, you indicated, until the end of March.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at that point you said you were discharged from that. Did you serve as head of the council any time after March, say in April, May, or June? Did you -- did they rename you head of that council after you were discharged in March?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A new order came on the appointment of the military administration, and the military administrators took over the whole thing. You can see that the council at that time no longer existed. But rather, we were distributed according to our sectors. My sector was economy, another person had public utility, so the whole thing no longer functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, okay. So there were no council meetings. You didn't attend any meetings as council president after you were discharged; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be called by the new commander of the military administration to attend meetings, but not all of us at once. He called whoever he needed at a certain point in time. Then he would call the person, talk to the person, and make certain agreements with that specific person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you had these meetings, did you ever have meetings with Blagoje Simic or any Crisis Staff members? Did they ever come to Odzak? We're talking in 1993. You mentioned you saw Blagoje Simic two or three times in 1992. Was Blagoje Simic there at meetings or visiting you in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the new commanders, they kept changing, and they would go to the seats of the municipalities, Samac, Modrica, or Brod. They would talk with the Executive Council and with the heads of municipalities. I'm not sure if Blagoje ever came in 1993. I can't be positive. Maybe he did, maybe he didn't. But as I no longer held that sort of a position in the new administration, I can't claim with any certainty whether he came in 1993 or not. Personally, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to have you look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If we can show it over the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at in a second the notes of Colonel Ratomir Simic, who you mentioned in your testimony on Thursday, and it relates to a meeting on the 12th of May, 1993. Can you see it, sir? Can you see it in front of you? I'm not sure if it's working?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Is it possible [inaudible] --

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you see the top where it says "12th of May, 1993," the third line down? Do you see the list of participants, the nine participants in the meeting, and number 2 is Savo Popovic, head of the Odzak military administration council?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then it says "Blagoje Simic, president of the Samac municipality." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, so you were president of the Odzak military administration council after March, after the end of March 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Blagoje Simic did attend this meeting with you. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I look at this document, yes, you can clearly see that there was a meeting. But it's been a long time, so I'm afraid I can't be very accurate. This means that there was a meeting, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, can you look at page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can I see the B/C/S equivalent, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to look at -- it looks like the first full paragraph on that page, or it could be the second paragraph on yours. It says: "In answer to General Subotic's question whether Odzak had been destroyed after the liberation and whether it could be settled with five to six thousand refugees, Savo Popovic replied that 80 to 90 per cent of the houses in Serbian villages had been destroyed, while in the Croatian villages, some houses remained intact, and building material should be taken from them, while the rest should be levelled to the ground." Do you recall saying that to General Subotic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. These are minutes, and I don't know what the person was taking the minutes said. I never saw this, nor did the person who was taking the minutes show me anything. I was talking about Serbian villages, you see, and said that Croatian villages were not levelled to the ground. I think that's a very arbitrary wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Because obviously, if the Croat homes were levelled, they couldn't be rebuilt or repaired; isn't that correct, sir, and these people could not come back?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Serbian and Croatian were destroyed, and yet, people came back. People repaired their houses. People brought along construction materials and they mended the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But if you level the Croat homes to the ground, you couldn't repair them; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I didn't myself take any part in the reparation of those buildings, so I can't talk from personal experience, because I was not the one destroying the buildings or the one issuing the orders for these buildings to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Objecting. It's for the third time that this witness said that, number one, he was not -- he didn't say that, that probably it's a construction of Colonel Simic. Secondly, that he was not involved in that, so I don't know why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, why are you interrupting? The witness was there. The witness knows what he's talking about. Let the witness answer, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I let him to answer Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just sit down. The questions are very clear. The witness is able to say whether he said anything like that which is recorded in this document. What's your problem? Mr. Weiner go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, Colonel Ratomir Simic, who drafted this document, he was the commander of the TG 1 military unit in Odzak; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the military administration and the commander of the TG.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to move the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked P169 and ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, are you continuing or you are through?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about people returning to Odzak. I have a few questions. Isn't it true that there were once thousands of non-Serbs, Muslims and Croats, living in Odzak, actually, tens of thousands were living in Odzak prior to July of -- maybe June or July of 1992? There were tens of thousands, or over 20.000, non-Serbs, meaning Muslims and Croats, living in Odzak; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the Odzak municipality, there were both Croats and Muslims, and Serbs living.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation didn't get the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were thousands --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, the interpreters said they didn't get the last part. Can the witness repeat his last answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters didn't receive the last part of your answer, could you repeat that again, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Croats and Muslims did live in Odzak municipality, but as far as I know, the Muslims only lived in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, weren't there -- regardless of where they lived in the municipality, weren't there thousands of non-Serbs living in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. How many exactly, I can't tell you off the top of my head, if there were 15 or 20,000 of them. But yes, there were quite many, and they were the predominant population in Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you agree, sir, that many of them, a large number, left as the Serb forces advanced and took over the town?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, before the Serb forces came, for a couple of days, both the Croats and Muslims left the area of Odzak municipality, perhaps on orders by the HVO or another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you agree that those who stayed, those Muslims and Croats who stayed, were forced out or killed by Serb forces? Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, according to my information, when the units of the 1st Krajina Corps came in, there were no Croats or Muslims there. Therefore, we can't talk about the use of force, if they had left the area, taking with them even a number of Serbs who were in prisons or camps. They took them to Brod and to other places in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, so you don't agree with that statement. Do you agree with the statement that the other non-Serbs were forced out after the Serbian population returned? Do you agree with that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs began to return after several days, following the release and the exchange that was done with the Croatian forces. Therefore, Serb retainees could not expel Croats or Muslims who were no longer there in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree that by the date of the signing of Dayton, out of the thousands or the large population of non-Serbs, few, if any, remained by that time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Dayton, in late 1993, I practically took up another position. I was a director in a company, and I was no longer involved and I no longer knew what happened as far as that area was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll get back to that in probably about a minute, but let me ask you this: You know Milan Simic, who was a defendant in this case? Do you know Milan?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Simic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was an economist and president of the Samac Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you testified that you had contact while you were on the council with the Samac Executive Board; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, as far as subordination or seniority is concerned, in the Crisis Staff, had we carried any real influence, then I probably wouldn't have gone to Milan to appeal for funds to be used for food for those who were returning to the Odzak area, in order to be better able to organise their life. That's what the contacts were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue our proceedings at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. Since we couldn't start right away because of the technical problems, you have another 20 minutes to complete your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's all I plan to use, is another 20 minutes, Your Honour. Thank you. I feel I should also be given some time to make up for the objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that you knew Milan Simic and that you had worked with him on some Odzak matters. Did Milan Simic help you or assist you at all?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He helped on our insistence, in terms of oil supply -- fuel supply and foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And whenever you called on Milan, was he pretty much always able to help you, or did he help you whenever he could?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were situations, objectively speaking, when he was able to, and sometimes when he didn't have it at his disposal, or the municipality didn't have it at its disposal. He did something when he was able to, whether he did it to the degree that was required, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you get along with Milan Simic, get along well with him?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any particular problems in relation to him personally. He did his work. I was elsewhere. So when we had dealings, that was an opportunity for us to be in contact, to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you trust him? Was he fair with you when you asked for things?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was his duty, as president of the Executive Board, to, whatever he was able to do, in terms of Samac municipality, helping for the people or to the people who were in the Odzak municipality, then he was fulfilling his duty, his obligations. There were situations when intervention should have been made, in the sense that pressure should have been exerted when there were shortages, and we needed things, so then sometimes there would just -- he would just have to insist on some requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you're aware that Milan Simic has pled guilty in this case and as part of his plea he's admitted to certain criminal activity. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read, and I wasn't -- I'm not aware of everything. I know that he was sentenced. I wasn't in touch with him so that I would know all the details. I just know that he was convicted and that he had partly accepted some responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, according to the sentencing judgement, at page 5, Milan Simic does not dispute and agrees that the government would have proven or that the Prosecution would have proven, paragraphs 36 and 37 of the indictment. And I have the B/C/S copy from the current indictment, which are the same paragraphs, registry's version, paragraphs 28 and 29 in B/C/S. And if you can look at those, I'd like to read those to you. In the fourth indictment that Milan Simic pled guilty to, he admitted to, paragraphs 36 and 37, which are 28 and 29 in the B/C/S version. You should have them on the ELMO, on the screen in front of you, sir. Can you see them? And I'd like to read those to you. Paragraph 36, which is your 28, paragraph in front of you: "On or about 13 July 1992, the 1st Krajina Corps of the Bosnian Serb army seized control of the neighbouring municipality of Odzak by force. As the Serb military forces advanced on Odzak, the majority of the non-Serb residents fled the area. Those non-Serbs who had not fled before the takeover fled, were killed, or were forced to leave." And I'll continue, paragraph 37, the next paragraph: "Prior to July 1992, approximately 22.500 Bosnian Croat Muslim residents, out of a population of 30.000, lived in Odzak municipality. In November of 1995 -- I'm sorry, in November 1995, at the time of the signing of the Dayton peace agreement, virtually all of the 22.500 Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim residents had fled or were forced to leave the municipality -- I'm sorry, the Odzak municipality." Did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that what happened? People either fled or they were forced to leave or killed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that people were forced. That's what we were told by the HVO, they were forced to leave, and that's what they did. But here, there's also talk of people being killed. If there were, I wouldn't have been able to know who, when this territory was being -- people being forced out of the territory, if Milan knew, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... is not accurate. Here it says, on page 35, "that's what we were told by the HVO," which would suggest that this witness was told by the HVO what happened, and this is not what he was testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think even the gaps, I think the interpreters didn't get everything. Can the witness simply repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also spoke previously that we had information at the Crisis Staff that the HVO had ordered people to leave the territory before the 1st Krajina Corps arrived, and practically all of the population were taken to the Croatian territory. I don't know anything about people killed, that there were people killed. That could have been -- could be known by those who participated in taking over of this territory, and I was not one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of Serb forces forcing people to leave -- forcing non-Serbian residents to leave Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, because we did not take part. Our units or Crisis Staff, they did not take part in taking over that territory, so I don't know whether there was or there wasn't. I can't possibly give an affirmative answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Biljana Plavsic has indicated that the Bosnian military police and civilian forces, under the control of the SDS and the Serbian leadership, collaborated with the JNA, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, and paramilitary units from within and outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to implement the objective of ethnic separation by force. That's what one of the Serbian leaders has stated as part of her plea of guilt. Isn't that consistent with Milan Simic's testimony that people were forced -- were killed or forced to leave Odzak? Isn't that consistent, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I don't believe that we heard the testimony of Mr. Milan Simic. If my learned friend makes certain references, it should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's plea agreement. It's plea agreement. You're wasting time, Mr. Pantelic. You're wasting my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because it's a public record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't the statement of Milan Simic in his plea agreement of people being forced to leave Odzak or being killed, these are non-Serbs, isn't that consistent with Biljana Plavsic's statement, factual statement for her plea that the JNA, the MUP, and many of these organisations collaborated to force non-Serbs to leave their municipalities? Isn't that consistent?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me to comment on what Biljana said in court. What Milan Simic said in court, and whether this is consistent or not. If you please, I cannot enter into details of what their testimony is and their behaviour, whether it's consistent or not. Probably they know why they said it, how they said it, and what kind of statements they gave. I don't see why I should offer any comment on that to say whether Milan is right or not and whether Biljana Plavsic said what she said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sir, the question is: Milan Simic's statement that people were forced to leave and Biljana Plavsic's statement that all these groups; the JNA, the MUP, the military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Milan Simic's statement that people were forced to leave and Biljana Plavsic's statement that it was a policy to force people to leave, aren't those consistent?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to object. The Prosecutor has now stated twice what Milan Simic said as his testimony. I have to put it on the record that the plea agreement is still under seal. Only parts that are in the verdict, in the judgement, can be quoted. The Prosecutor should quote anything to do with the judgement, but the entire plea agreement and the testimony of Milan Simic is under seal. I would like the Prosecutor to be very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 5 of the judgement indicates which facts and allegations Milan Simic agrees to, and it says: "Paragraphs 28 to 30, 32 to 34 and 36 to 37 of the indictment," and that's exactly what I just read to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just as it states in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps Mr. Lukic should be more careful in looking at the documents the Prosecution is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So once again. One last time, sir. Milan Simic's statement that the non-Serbs of Odzak were killed or forced to leave, isn't that consistent with Biljana Plavsic's statement that it was a policy to force the non-Serbs of certain municipalities to leave? Aren't those two consistent?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, when you're speaking about the statements or the testimonies, I don't know what Milan Simic had as data, that in the municipality of Odzak non-Serbs were killed. Where did he get the information? What was the number of non-Serbs killed? At this very moment, I cannot even know whether there were murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question --

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let alone whether that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not my question. The my question is: Are those two statements consistent? Just whether or not they're consistent. I'm not asking you to examine the factual basis of each. Are those two statements consistent?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer by profession to offer comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, that is not a question for a lawyer. That is just a matter of language. The Prosecution is asking you whether the two statements are consistent, that's all. You can easily answer that.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said, they have similarities in the statements, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let's go to the last issue. We've had a number of witnesses testify in this case concerning looting in Odzak. You've even admitted as to looting or robberies in Odzak; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was taking away of property from companies, as well as from private homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, while you were in Odzak, Simo Zaric was also in Odzak, in an intelligence position; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in that position, in intelligence, it was his job to find out what was happening within the Odzak community; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had to if he was doing certain work, as much as he had access to, he had to cooperate with me in terms of security and the army. But in those relationships --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we lost your statement after you said, "in those relationships," after you indicated he had to cooperate with you and the army in terms of security. Could you repeat the rest of your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these relationships, I don't know how much they agreed, and in terms of all this, he didn't have to inform me, because I was not -- that was not my position of authority for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, my question to you is: It was his job to find out what was happening in Odzak; isn't that correct, as an intelligence -- as the intelligence specialist for the council? That was his job, to find out what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was supposed to find out, but what he -- whether he was in a position to do that, considering that this territory was, as I said, almost hermetically closed, that each brigade had its area of responsibility, they had their own security organs. How much Simo managed to get to certain information, to certain intelligence, and to get into these areas, he's the one who should know best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, since he was in the area of intelligence and it was his job to gather information, he was in a better position than you to know what was happening in relation to these military and civilian crimes; isn't that correct? He's out there trying to obtain information, so he's in a better position than you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly he was better informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could the witness see 142 ter, pages 137 and 138. The bottom of page 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Mr. Zaric has given a statement in June of 1998 and actually his second statement in April of 1998, and in both statements he indicated that the Crisis Staff was responsible for the organised looting of the town of Odzak? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, that the Crisis Staff was responsible. I don't know for which part was he responsible for, if it was military administration, headed by -- that is, that this was for the part of the Odzak municipality. They had complete authority, they had under its control. So I don't see how Crisis Staff could have been responsible and could have been conducting the lootings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let's read -- if you follow in B/C/S on the bottom of 137 into page 138. In the English I'll read, which is on page 138. Zaric's statement, which is P142 ter. "I know that we found Odzak when we arrived as a military council, the many goods when the Croatian forces were retreating was taken from Odzak from the factories and so on. And that a large amount of goods still remained in the factory. We had a commission, as a military council, which went from company to company, and wrote down the machines, what was there in terms of finished products, in what state it was, how much wheat or corn there was in the silos, how many domestic animals there were in the ranches and the farms, and this military council who wrote all this down, and through commander Popovic, transferred it to the Crisis Staff in Samac, and every day it was organised through the Executive Council and their institutions. They took these machines and these goods. They say that they sold them and gave up some of these goods so that the army of the Republika Srpska could be fed. But I believe that a large amount went into their pockets -- went in their pockets, of which I have no physical evidence, but it went that way because it was looted, and that's the way things were done during this war." So you -- question: "So you had no knowledge of this looting while it was going on and were not involved?" Answer: "When I talk about this looting, I said it was done in an organised manner, and I participated in no looting whatsoever, not even a plastic cup like this. Much less ordered anybody else to do so." Sir, do you agree with Mr. Zaric that the Crisis Staff was involved in the looting in Odzak? Do you agree with that, sir? You were a member of the Crisis Staff. Were you and the other members of the Crisis Staff involved in the looting of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part, and I could not have taken part in looting with the Crisis Staff. When talking about organised looting, no machine or anything else could have been taken out without the approval of the commander of the military administration. So if anybody wanted from Samac or Modrica -- I don't know whether you hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, I heard you. And Zaric also states, on the 2nd of April, 1998: Question: "So this is the Samac Crisis Staff who was allowing this looting to go on?" Answer: "Yes. Many things were taken away. It was all organised by them." Sir, that's P141 ter, page 94. Were you and the Crisis Staff involved in that looting, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you can't answer that question in the affirmative, you can't answer that question in the affirmative, or you would be incriminating yourself in a war crime, isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say the following: That if anybody, according to the instructions that were at the time, if that person came to Odzak, and if that person wanted to take some goods, and if he went to the military administration, he would have to supply a request, submit a request, and say that he needed something for a specific purpose. And then if that was approved, he would then have to obtain a certain certificate, a document. That would be recorded. And then that person would take that machine or something else, that person would then take that machine or something else to Modrica or to Samac. Now, if he did something else further with that machine or that other thing, I don't know. I was not in a position whether that was taken somewhere else, I was not in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, was: Isn't it true that you cannot answer the question about the involvement of the Crisis Staff in looting in the affirmative or you would be incriminating yourself? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I could incriminate myself if, as a man who was there in Odzak, I directly requested or submitted requests for certain things that I needed. But did I participate in such a way that I would prepare certain documents that were submitted to the command of the military administration to be approved? But this was just the military field of authority, whether they would give it to you or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've indicated that Simo Zaric, because of his position in intelligence, was in a better position than you to know what was going on, and you agree with me that he has indicated or he has indicated in his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that the Crisis Staff was involved in the organised looting of Odzak? Do you agree with me in that statement that I've just read to you, that Simo Zaric, who was in a better position, who you've admitted was in a better position than you to know what was going on has indicated that the Crisis Staff was involved in the looting? Isn't that correct? That's what Zaric has stated.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Simo Zaric was in a position to know and to monitor certain developments, then he should specify what the names were of people from the Crisis Staff who took part in organised looting. And just on whose orders something was taken from Odzak then he should know where this thing ended up, if someone had taken anything away from Odzak, on an individual basis or collectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question to you is: You've admitted that Simo Zaric was in a better position than you to know what was going on with regard to crimes and looting, and he has indicated that the Crisis Staff was involved with the looting of Odzak. Isn't that true? Isn't that correct, that he has said that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's his opinion. I don't have a single piece of evidence that would confirm that any members of the Crisis Staff appropriated or misappropriated anything, or that they had taken anything away from Odzak pursuant to any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But as you previously said, sir, you weren't in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
